concepts.title: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation' refers to.
questions.a: The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty from the monarch to a body of French citizens, introducing measures like the ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen), a new tricolour flag, and an elected body called the Assembly, marking the first clear expression of nationalism in Europe.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation'.
questions.a: The French Revolution established that a nation is not the property of a king but a community of equal citizens who together constitute the sovereign power.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation

concepts.title: The Making of Nationalism in Europe

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Making of Nationalism in Europe' refers to.
questions.a: Nationalism in Europe emerged through a long process: the decline of feudalism, the growth of new trade and a middle class, the rise of the nation-state, and the cultural movements of Romanticism, all of which gradually replaced the multi-national empires with states built around a shared identity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Making of Nationalism in Europe'.
questions.a: No nation-state existed in mid-eighteenth-century Europe; nationalism grew out of social, economic and cultural changes that slowly created shared identities among people who had previously identified with local regions or empires.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Making of Nationalism in Europe' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Making of Nationalism in Europe

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Age of Revolutions (1830-1848)' refers to.
questions.a: The period 1830-1848 saw a wave of revolutions across Europe driven by liberal-nationalists and republicans; the July Revolution of 1830 in France, the Greek war of independence, and the revolutions of 1848 all aimed to establish constitutional government and national unity, though most were suppressed by conservative forces.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Age of Revolutions (1830-1848)'.
questions.a: Even though the revolutions of 1830-1848 largely failed to achieve their immediate political goals, they spread nationalist and liberal ideas across Europe and weakened the conservative order established by the Congress of Vienna.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Age of Revolutions (1830-1848)' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Age of Revolutions (1830-1848)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Unification of Germany' refers to.
questions.a: Germany was unified in 1871 under the leadership of Prussia's Chief Minister Otto von Bismarck, who used the Prussian army and bureaucracy along with three wars -- against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870-71) -- to unite the German states into a powerful empire, proclaimed at Versailles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Unification of Germany'.
questions.a: The unification of Germany was achieved not by popular democratic movements but by the Prussian state using military power and diplomacy under Bismarck's policy of 'blood and iron'.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Unification of Germany' taught, and from which source text?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Unification of Italy' refers to.
questions.a: Italy was unified in 1861-1870 through the efforts of Count Camillo de Cavour (Chief Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont), Giuseppe Garibaldi and Giuseppe Mazzini; Cavour used diplomacy and war, Garibaldi led armed volunteers, and in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of united Italy, with Rome added in 1870.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Unification of Italy'.
questions.a: Unlike Germany's top-down military unification, Italy's unification combined diplomatic manoeuvring, popular armed struggle and the idealism of Mazzini's Young Italy movement, but ordinary people remained largely excluded from the new nation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Unification of Italy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Making of Germany and Italy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nationalism and Imperialism' refers to.
questions.a: By the last quarter of the nineteenth century, nationalism in Europe had shifted from a liberating force to a justification for imperial expansion; the great powers -- Britain, France, Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary -- competed for colonies in Africa and Asia, driven by national pride, economic interests and the balance of power.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nationalism and Imperialism'.
questions.a: Nationalism, which began as a movement for freedom and self-determination, was transformed into an ideology of imperial rivalry that ultimately led to the First World War.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nationalism and Imperialism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Visualising the Nation and Nationalism and Imperialism

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Balkan Crisis' refers to.
questions.a: The Balkan region, comprising modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, was under Ottoman control and became a site of intense nationalist tension as the Slavic peoples sought independence; the rivalry of great powers over this region led to a series of wars and ultimately to the First World War.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Balkan Crisis'.
questions.a: The Balkans became a powder keg because each great power tried to control the region for its own strategic and economic interests, while the newly independent Balkan states themselves competed for territory, making the area the flashpoint of the First World War.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Balkan Crisis' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Nationalism and Imperialism - The Balkans

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Visualising the Nation' refers to.
questions.a: Artists in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries personified nations as female figures that stood as allegories of the nation's ideas -- Marianne for France, Germania for Germany -- using symbols like the tricolour, red cap, sword and crown of oak leaves to convey abstract ideas of liberty, justice and unity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Visualising the Nation'.
questions.a: Since a nation is an abstract idea, artists used female allegorical figures with specific symbols to give concrete visual form to the values and identity of the nation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Visualising the Nation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Visualising the Nation
